A1.justification: Both PDFs contain the same survey, with readable text, equations, figures and tables. v1 ends with references; v3 adds Appendix A. The retained material and additions can be reliably matched across the changed layout.

before.justification: v1 presents a literature taxonomy and explanatory illustrations. Its example images are attributed to cited papers; no original experimental or data-analysis outcomes are reported.

after.justification: Appendix Figures 11–15 present comparative model outputs, but their captions and Section 2.3 do not establish whether the authors generated these outputs or collected them from other sources. No experimental setup resolves their provenance. Figures 16–17 are described as representative outputs from existing works.

M1.justification: Neither version proposes a new synthesis algorithm. The three denoising-network stages and six sampling mechanisms are retained. Newly reviewed architectures and revised descriptions of existing methods do not constitute changes to a method proposed by this survey.

E1.justification: The seven surveyed task categories are retained. Appendix Figures 11–15 add examples within these categories, but their datasets and sample provenance are unspecified, preventing a reliable judgment about additional actual evaluation coverage. Video, 3D and motion synthesis are discussed as extensions rather than evaluated tasks.

E2.justification: v3 introduces explicit visual comparison groups in Figures 11–15, absent from v1. Examples include SR3, SRDiff, DDRM and DPS for restoration, and Prompt-to-Prompt, Plug-and-Play, MasaCtrl, Imagic and RF-edit for editing. These are newly presented comparisons, although most participants were already discussed in v1.

E3.justification: The new appendix comparisons organize outputs around common displayed inputs: six text prompts in Figure 11, six restoration sources in Figure 12 and six editing instructions in Figure 13. This adds a limited qualitative comparison design, without specifying quantitative metrics, data splits, sampling settings or training budgets.

E4.justification: Neither version supplies ablations, sensitivity sweeps or dedicated robustness experiments. The new appendix panels show task outputs without a separate diagnostic analysis. The robustness section remains a discussion of field-wide challenges and possible remedies.

E5.justification: Neither version reports an experimental repeated-run methodology, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. Additional displayed samples do not establish a change in uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Appendix Figures 11–17 add numerous concrete qualitative outputs and comparisons beyond v1's illustrative examples, including text generation, restoration, editing and customization results. There are no numerical benchmark tables or sufficiently documented conditions to establish controlled performance gains or aggregate rankings.

T1.justification: Sections 2.1.2 and 2.4 add explicit mathematical connections between noise prediction and scaled scores, and between classifier-free guidance, a strengthened target density and a likelihood ratio. The core diffusion equations and existing theoretical arguments remain; the newly displayed conditional loss restates an existing objective.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains the same taxonomy of conditioning mechanisms. v3's introduction additionally claims applicability to video, 3D and motion synthesis, while its conclusion adds unified MLLM-based conditional synthesis as a research direction.

C2.justification: New Tables 2–3 systematically compare computational costs, applicability and claimed synthesis guarantees. Section 4.2 adds an explanation of attention replacement's restrictions on non-rigid editing. Section 5.6 introduces MLLM limitations and a hypothesis about lost local detail, while Section 2.3 qualifies the comparability of composition and layout examples.

D1.justification: The appendix newly supplies exact prompts and model-version labels such as SD-1.5 and SD-2.1. Section 2.2 also expands architectural details, including time embeddings and residual/self-attention blocks. Reproduction instructions for the visual comparisons remain absent, and the reviewed-works repository link is unchanged.

R1.justification: The survey substantially expands its discussion of DiT, Cross-DiT, MMDiT, Flux and flow matching, alongside additional inverse-problem and guidance work such as ReSample, DAPS, DiffPIR and TFG. New references also connect image conditioning to video, 3D and motion synthesis. These extend the research synthesis beyond bibliographic updates.

P1.justification: Substantial rewriting spans the introduction, architecture background, restoration, encoders and inversion discussions. Basic classifier and classifier-free guidance material is reorganized into Section 2.4, and Section 5.6 and an appendix are added. The overall taxonomy remains recognizable despite extensive editorial revision.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout. v1 Figure 2 is split into v3 Figures 4 and 8; Table I's method references move to Appendix Table 4. v3 adds a U-Net diagram, redraws the workflow illustration, adds comparison Tables 2–3 and introduces Appendix Figures 11–17.

improvement.justification: v3 improves accessibility and currency through clearer background explanations, expanded DiT/flow coverage and explicit mechanism comparisons. The visual examples also aid understanding. These benefits are limited by undocumented comparison provenance and settings, mismatched model references in Figure 11, and Figures 16–17 being captioned as customization despite illustrating composition and layout control.
